ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Saraswati Heritage Project 
*61. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
CULTURE be pleased to state the progress made in the project on unearthing the 
Saraswati River Heritage Project? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): No sanction order 
in regard to Sarasvati Heritage Project was issued. The Project Report was prepared in 
September 2003 envisaging a cost of Rs. 36.02 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 
4.98 crores as reflected in the financial concurrence accorded on 01.03.2004. This 
amount was to be met from the regular budgetary provisions. 
In anticipation of sanction of the project, six sites were taken up for excavation in 
the year 2003-04, in addition to three sites which had been taken up earlier. The 
excavations are in progress. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY:  Sir, this is the most 
important project. Normally, there is a practice followed in our country that whenever a 
new Government assumes office, they will be undoing all the previous projects since they 
have their own priorities. But here is a project which the former Minister, Jagmohanji, has 
initiated, and he has done a lot of good work since it has got its own importance. Sir, the 
unearthing of the Sarasvati River route had a close link with the ancient Harappan 
civilisation. I would like to know from the hon. Minister the details of the sites excavated so 
far for exploration work, and the results achieved. 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, as I mentioned in my written answer, the then 
Government accorded financial sanction on 1st March, 2004 by which time the 
elections had been announced. The Re port as such was prepared only in 
September, 2003 envisaging a cost of Rs. 36.02 crores, which was reduced, in 
just three months, to Rs. 4.98 crores. In fact, no Sanction Order was issued. It 
all confined to files. But as I said, we were taking up excavations, six sites were 
taken up for excavation in 2003-04. Earlier, three sites has been taken up. 
Excavations on all the sites will be in progress, and they are in progress. Sir, 
all these sites, nine, are part of, what may be considered, Harappan Zone. Since 
Harappa and Mohanjodro are in Pakistan, we wanted to know as an independent 
India as to whether they were zones in our part of the country, and we did find, we 
did excavate Dholavera site, to a great extent. We found a lot of archaeological 
objects which were datable to pre-Harappan, Harappan historical periods. But, 
Sir, this has nothing to do with the Sarasvati River Project as such. These 
excavations will go on. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, my second 
supplementary is, whether several pre- Harappan sites have been found while 
exploring the roots of rivers and whethe r the Archaeological Survey of India 
would be asked to quicken the work on important heritage projects to build tourist 
hubs and develop the new places excavated for attracting tourists. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: First of all, Sir, as for tourist hub sites, this is a 
project taken up by the Tourism Ministry. At the time, Jagmohanji was 
handling both the Ministries. Therefore, I am afraid, I am not competent to answer 
the question. However, I said that the work was going on at all the nine sites 
because we want to know the facts. Nobody should hesitate to know the facts. 
Facts, in my view, are sacred. 
SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether he knows that a very deep and extensive study was done by one 
Vedic scholar, Shri K.K. Sastri, of Ahmedabad. He is 100 years old. He has 
recently written a book on "Saraswati". He visited all the nine sites. He has also 
given some indications in his book. I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
whether he or his Department or his Ministry would make a study of the contents 
of that book and pursue the contents of that book. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, I have not read the book. The literature so far 
available does indicate that all these nine sites could be considered 
2 

[6 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
either pre-Harappan or Harappan or historical sites. They are all of high 
archaeological value. My only appeal to  the Members is not to confuse the 
archaeological value with a particular kind of project. 
DR. K. KASTURIRANGAN: Sir, I just want to bring, through you, to the 
attention of the hon. Minister that th e study from space revealed the existence 
of an ancient riverine system. Whether it is Sarawati or not, it is not important. The 
second component is that there are conjectures regarding the way it disappeared, 
including the violent plate tectonic movements in that region. The third 
component is hydrology, the potential of water, in case the riverine system had 
contributed to the subterranean ducts. Last one, of course, is archaeology. Any 
study which is related to the archaeological site excavation should also be 
suplemented and complemented by the other disciplines and it could be a very nice 
integrated study of that region from several of these disciplines point of view. I 
would request the hon. Minister to consider it as a proposal. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I think it is a good suggestion. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, I take all the facts mentioned by the hon. 
Member, who is one of our eminent scientists, very seriously. We will think 
of an inter-discjplinary study. At the moment, we are engaged in excavations. 
As and when the facts of excavation warrant such a study, we will not hesitate 
to take up such a study. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Hon. Chairman, Sir, may I ask, through you, the 
hon. Minister whether the procedure, as I understand it, of finalising sites for 
excavation is on the basis of proposals from certain stipulated organisations like 
Universities, State Governments and academic bodies? Then there is the Central 
Advisory Board which advises the Archaeological Survey of India on the 
excavation. I would like to know from the hon. Minister as to who mooted the 
original proposal for the so-called Saraswati River Project to which the question 
refers. What was the date on which the Central Advisory Board came to this 
conclusion that these were the sites which were to be excavated? 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, the then Minister took some initiative in the 
matter in December, 2002, if I recall correctly. I don't have those dates with me. 
Later, it was referred to the Central Advisory Board of Archaeologists. They also 
cleared it. Even otherwise, we are guided by the advice of this Board. I am trying 
to differentiate excavation from the speci fic project. As and when the data 
thrown up warrants such a project, I will certainly commission the project. At 
the moment, I do not find any need for it. 
3 

RAJYA  SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, the Minister has not answered my question. I want the 
specific name of the body which proposed it and on the basis of which the Central Advisory 
Board took cognizance of that proposal. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: The Minister, at that time, formed a Committee with himself as 
the Chairperson for this purpose and took a view on the file; while no decision 
materialised in the form of sanction. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: The disappearance of the River Saraswati is one of the great 
mysteries of our archaeology and of our history because from the Sangam, the Ganga, the 
Yamuna and the Saraswati, W&R\ ST^T^I M % I Where did it go? How did it go? The 
Minsiter has said that it is only after the excavation that he would consider an integrated 
project as suggested by one of the hon. Members. My submission is this. Wouldn't the 
Minister like to do the two things simultaneously? You can do remote sensing, you can do 
satellite photography and you can also do excavations so that if there is a link between the 
disappeared river and the archaeological sites, that can be found. They don't have to come 
seriatim, perhaps they can go contiguously. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, the suggestion will be studied. But as of now, we have 
only found archaeological objects whose dates can be traced to pre-Harappa and Harappa culture. 
There are certain rivulets now. Beyond that there is not enough evidence to show that a particular 
river had existed in the past.

Protection of ancient religious places and temples in Uttaranchal 
†*62. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the names of the ancient religious places and temples of Uttaranchal protected by 
the Archaeological Survey of India; 
(b) whether his Ministry is working on the schemes for protection and development 
of these places; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof together with the amount spent for this purpose during 
the last two years, year-wise and the amount proposed to be spent during the year 
2004-05? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) to (c) A Statement 
is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
Protection of ancient religious places and temples in Uttaranchal 
(a) There are 44 centrally protected monuments under the jurisdiction of Dehradun 
Circle of Archaeological Survey of India in the State of

*67. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA. Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased testate: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to the National Centre for Promotion of Employment 
for Disabled people, only 1.2 per cent of the disabled in the country has had any 
form of education; 
(b) whether his Ministry has any statistics as to how many disabled students are 
studying in 322-odd universities in the country; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN 
SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The Persons with Disabilities (Equal opportunities, Protection of Rights and 
Full Participation) Act, 1995 provides that all Government educational institutions and 
other educational institutions receiving aid 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
from the Government, shall reserve not less than three per cent seats for persons with 
disabilities. The National Centre for Promotion of Employment for Disabled People 
(NCPEDP), a Non-Governmental organization, has informed the Central Government 
about the survey conducted by it among Universities, a sample of colleges and schools; to 
assess the status of mainstream education of students with disabilities. According to 
the NCPEDP, the enrolment of students with disabilities in 119 respondent Universities 
was only about 1635 students, constituting only about 0.1 per cent of the total enrolment of 
the responding Universities. 
Similarly, the NCPEDP has reported that according to its survey only 679 students 
with disabilities were enrolled in 96 responding colleges, constituting only 0.52 per cent 
of the total enrolment in these colleges. The NCPEDP survey on enrolment of students 
with disabilities in schools has concluded that only 382 students with disabilities were 
enrolled in 89 responding schools, which was only 0.51 per cent of the total students 
enrolled in those schools. The survey conducted by NCPEDP pertains to the low levels of 
curent enrolment of students with disabilities in mainstream education. 
With regard to the enrolment of students in the University system, the University 
Grants Commission (UGC) is in the process of collecting information from all 
Universities, Deemed to be Universities and over 15,500 colleges in the country. The UGC 
has so far received information for 115 universities, according to which the enrolment of 
students with disabilities in University Teaching Departments is only 2156 constituting 
0.33 per cent of the total enrolment in the said Universities. Thus, according to the survey 
conducted by the NGO, NCPEDP as well as the available information with the UGC, the 
current enrolment of students with disabilities falls far short of the statutory 
requirement of 3 per cent. 
In respect of access of students with disabilities to the 'secondary and above level' of 
education, according to the National Sample Survey (58th Round) estimate for the period 
July to December, 2002, the number of disabled persons in the country was 18.53 
million-forming about 1.8 per cent of the total population-of whom about 9 per cent 
have completed their 'secondary and above level' of education. 
In order to encourage greater participation by children with disabilities at various levels 
of education, the Central Government provides financial assistance under the Sarva 
ShikshaAbhiyan for elementary schooling, the Integrated Education for the Disabled 
Children (IEDC) for integration 
24 

[6 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
of children with disabilities in secondary schools, and under the scheme of the UGC 
relating to higher Education for Persons with Special Needs.

Statement 
National Policy for Senior Citizens 
In pursuance to the National Policy on Older Persons, the Government has set 
up a National Council for Older Persons (NCOP) under the Chairmanship of 
Minister (SJ&E) in 1999. The NCOP is broad-based to advise and coordinate 
with the Government in the formulation and implementation of National Policy 
and programmes for the welfare of the aged. The Council also works as a nodal 
point at the national level for redressing the grievances of older persons and to 
represent their collective opinion to the Government 
Besides, the Ministry has also set up an Inter Ministerial Committee (IMC) 
headed by Secretary (SJ&E) with the sole aim of effective implementation of 
the National Policy on Older Persons and for taking action on the 
recommendations of NCOP. The Ministry periodically reviews progress on the 
implementation of the National Policy on Older Persons through meetings of 
NCOP and IMC. The last meeting of the IMC was held on 30.11.2004. 
Some of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India concerned 
with the welfare of senior citizens are extending various facilities/ concessions for 
the welfare of older persons which are as under: 
Financial Security 
Income Tax rebate of upto Rs. 20,000 or actual tax whichever is less is allowed 
to senior citizens who have attained the age of 65 years, thereby exempting 
annual income upto Rs. 1.53 lakh from income tax. 
For Senior Citizens, deduction in respect of medical insurance premia upto 
Rs. 15,000/- is allowed while calculating the taxable income. 
A Special Senior Citizens Savings Scheme with provision of higher 
interest. 
45 

RAJYA SABHA          [6 December, 2004] 
Under the Old Age Pension Scheme, monthly pension is given at variable rates to 
the destitute old. The number of persons covered under the scheme during 2001-02 
was around 54.30 lakh,. 
Health Security 
Medical insurance like Mediclaim Policy is available for senior citizens up to 
75 years of age Universal Health Insurance Scheme for senior citizens upto 75 
years of age. 
Separate queues for older persons in hos pitals for registration and cilinical 
examination. 
Evening OPDs for the elderly in some government hospitals. 
Development of training module for doctors in the care of the elderly. 
Food Security 
Antyodaya Scheme: 2 crore families from amongst those with income below 
the poverty line have been covered under the Targeted Public Distribution 
System. 35 kg of food grains are provided  to each eligible family at a highly 
subsidized rate. The elderly members of such families benefit from this 
assistance. 
Annapoorna Scheme: 10 kgs. of food grains per person per month is 
provided free of cost to those senior citizens who remain uncovered under 
the old age pension scheme.  
Concessions in travel 
Reservation of two seats for senior citizens in front row of the public buses. 
Indian Railways provide 30% fare concession in all trains for senior 
citizens aged 60 years and above. 
50 per cent Senior Citizens discount on air fares subject to certain 
conditions. 
Separate counters for Senior Citizens for purchase/booking/cancellation of 
tickets. 
Other provisions 
Cells for redressal of grievances of the elderly in government departments. Early 
hearing of court cases involving older persons.

Financial assistance is provided to Non Governmental Organisations for 
construction and maintenance of old age homes, day care centres and mobile 
medicare units by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. 
Legal provisions for protection of older persons from physical and 
emotional abuse and domestic violence. 
A rebate of 30% of the tax due on the covered space of such building up to one 
hundred sq. mtrs. of the covered space has been allowed by the Municipal 
Corporation of Delhi in the case of any self-occupied residential building singly 
owned by a man who is sixty years or more in age. 
Under Section 125 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 every person having 
sufficient means is required to maintain the parents if they are unable to 
maintain themselves. 
The Ministry has requested all State Governments to frame their State Policy 
on Older Persons. So far, the State Governments of Karnataka and Goa have 
already announced their State Policy for Older Persons. 
Further as per the directions of this Ministry, the Director Generals of Police

formations about special attention to be paid for safeguarding the lives and 
properties of senior citizens.

Quality standards for agricultural products 
306. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the countries signatory to the World Trade Organisation's 
Agreement on Agriculture have prescribed specific quality and 
sanitary/phyto sanitary standards for different agricultural produce they 
import; 
(b) if so, whether these standards are uniform and identical for all the 
countries of origin; 
 
(c) what are the standards for the commodities exported by India; 
(d) what are the facilities, like testing laboratories, available to farmers in 
the country; 
(e) whether Government propose to extend and improve these testing 
facilities; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) Members of the 
World Trade Organization (WTO) have undertaken to subscribe to the 
Agreement establishing the WTO along with other annexed multilateral 
Agreements, including th e Agreement on Agricultu re and the Agreement on 
Sanitary and Phyto-Sanitary Measures  (SPS), in the form of a 'single 
undertaking'. As per the SPS Agreement,  Member countries are expected to 
harmonize their standards with international standards (Codex Alimentarius 
Commission for human health, International Plant Protection Convention 
(IPPC) for plant health and International Office of Epizootics (OIE) for 
animal health). The SPS Agreement, however, provid es that in case more 
stringent standards are applied by any country, these have to be based on 
scientific principles and risk analys is. Members shall ensure that their 
sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures do not arbitrarily or unjustifiably 
53 

RAJYA SABHA  [6 December, 2004] 
discriminate between members were identical or similar conditions prevail, 
including between their own territory and that of other members. Sanitary and 
phytosanitary measures shall not be applied in a manner which would constitute a 
disguised restriction on international trade. 
(c) Under the Export (Quality Control & Inspection) Act, 1963, at present there 
are 6 product groups that are covered under compulsory export quality control and 
inspection. These products include fish and fishery products, dairy products, egg 
products, poultry products, meat products and honey. Notifications have been brought out 
subjecting these products to mandatory quality control and inspection prior to 
export. The standards applicable have been generally laid down which inter alia 
include: (i) National standards of importing country, (ii) Contractual 
specifications agreed to between the foreign buyer and the exporters provided that 
the same satisfies the health and other requirements of the importing country and (iii) 
in the absence of these two, the minimum specifications laid down in the 
notifications, The standards broadly cover the physical and chemical parameters as 
well as residues for pesticides, veterinary drugs, heavy metals etc. which are 
specified in the notifications. 
(d) In order to improve the testing facilities, the Government of India have already 
set up/strengthened a Central Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (Izatnagar, Bareilly) 
and four Regional Disease Diagnostic Laboratories (Jallandhar, Pone, Bangalore and 
Kolkata). Ultra-modern Plant Quarantine Laboratory facilities are established at the 
five (5) major Plant Quarantine Stations (Amritsar, Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai and 
New Delhi) for undertaking Quarantine inspection and testing of agricultural 
commodities either imported into or exported out of the country. 
(e) and (f) Yes, improvement of the testing laboratories and related facilities is a 
constant endeavour of the Government. It has been proposed, under, the Tenth 
Plan, to strengthen further Quarantine laboratory facilities for inspection of 
agricultural commodities at the other major/minor ports:

Free Trade Agreement with Thailand 
315. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has signed Free Trade Agreement with Thailand; 
(b) if so, salient features thereof; 
(c) whether the Indian industries have expressed apprehension about the entire 
process of this agreement; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) Government's reaction thereto? 
63 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRf E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) No, Sir. However, 
India and Thailand have signed only a Framework Agreement for establishing a Free 
Trade Area (FTA) on 9th October 2003 in Bangkok, Thailand. The key elements 
of the Framework Agreement cover FTA in Goods, Services and Investment, and 
Areas of Economic Cooperation. The Framework Agreement also provides for 
an Early Harvest Scheme (EHS) under which common items have been agreed 
for elimination of tariffs on a fast track basis. 
(c) to (e) The list of items on which tariff concessions will be exchanged 
between India and Thailand under the Early Harvest Scheme has been finalized 
after consultations with the administra tive Ministries/Departments and the 
domestic stakeholders. The tariff preferences on imports to India would be 
available only for those products which enjoy the 'originating status' in 
Thailand as prescribed under the Rules of Origin which are integral part of any Free 
Trade Agreement. Similarly, the products which enjoy the 'originating status' in 
India would only get tariff preferences for imports in Thailand. To protect the 
vulnerable sections of the domestic industry, the Framework Agreement 
provides for each country to maintain a negative/ sens itive list of items on 
which no tariff concessions shall be granted under the FTA. In addition, the 
Agreement provides for trade defence measures which an importing country 
can take recourse to. In case of a surge in imports and injury to the domestic 
industry, a country is allowed to take measures such as anti-dumping and 
safeguards. The Agreement also provides for cooperation among customs 
authorities for ensuring that the Rules are not violated.

Non-tariff barriers on agricultural exports 
326. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a)' whether it is a fact that the countries signatory to the Agreement on Agriculture 
under the World Trade Organisation (WTO) have prescribed different kinds of non-tariff 
barriers with a view to restricting their imports into their territories; and 
(b) if so, the details of the non-tariff barriers prescribed by the countries importing 
agricultural produce from India in respect of these commodities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 
(SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) The Most Favoured Nation (MFN) Treatment 
requirement of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) does not permit any 
discrimination or restriction specific to Indian goods by other WTO Members. Moreover, 
WTO rules allow restrictions on imports of goods based on tariffs as agreed upon and also 
through specific non-tariff measures, including those based on balance of payment grounds, 
sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures, conformity with agreed/international standards and 
contingent protection measures like anti-dumping, subsidy and safeguard actions. 
Nevertheless, non-tariff barriers, beyond agreed WTO rules, exist on import of goods 
from India in some WTO Member countries, including maintenance of sanitary and 
phyto-sanitary measurs at levels which are not readily justifiable on the basis of 
scientific evidence. Procedural requirements could also act as barriers to trade. Problems 
arising due to non-tariff barriers are duly taken up by Government with the concerned 
authorities of the country concerned either bilaterally with a view to their early and 
mutually satisfactory resolution or presented for resolution by the WTO's Dispute 
Settlement Mechanism. In the ongoing W TO negotiations, India has also co-sponsored 
proposals alongwith some other developing countries to disallow use of measures by 
developed countries that act as barriers to imports from developing countries.

World Heritage Sites 
340. SHRI R.P GOENKA: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the UNESCO has proposed to classify some of the 
world heritage sites in India, including Hampi in Karnataka, in the "endangered" 
category; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including the specific messages/warnings conveyed by the 
UN agency and the steps being taken to preserve the integrity, of the archaeological 
sites by saving them from any physical harm or compromising their unique ambience 
and scenic surroundings? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The World Heritage Committee has placed two World Heritage sites-the 
Group of Monuments at Hampi and the Manas Wild Life Sanctuary-in the 
endangered category. As far as the archaeological site of Hampi is concerned, it was 
put in list of danger in 1999 due to construction of a bridge across the river 
Tungabhadra in the core zone area of the site. Two UNESCO Missions have visited 
the site and suggested corrective measures. The important suggestions are: 
(a) to construct a road by passing the core zone 
(b) to prepare a comprehensive site management plan 
(c) to include local communities in the development programmes envisaged at 
the site etc. 
The Government of Karnataka has taken steps to construct the new By-pass road by 
acquiring requisite land and the work is in progress. School of Planning and 
Architecture, New Delhi is entrusted with the work of formulating comprehensive 
site management plan to address 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
various issues relating to development and to maintain the integrity and authenticity of 
the World Heritage Site. 
Archaeological Survey of India in association with Government of Karnataka is 
making all. efforts to implement the recommendations and corrective measures suggested 
by the World Heritage Committee. 
Manas Wild Life Sanctuary was put in danger list in 1992. The World Heritage Centre 
approved a rehabilitation plan and agreed to provide, international assistance. The World 
Heritage Committee in its 28th session recommended: 
(i)  to undertake a mission to assess the security situation and ecological 
conditions 
(ii)  to begin activities benefiting the site as soon as possible. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forest has been working with World Heritage 
Centre, United Nations Foundation and other national and international partner* 
to raise financing and activate conservation works.

Transfer of teachers in Kenariya Vidyalayas 
375. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have found clear cut evidence that irregular 
procedure was adopted in the past to affect transfer of Kendriya Vidyalaya 
teachers; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to rectify the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) Transfers made under 
the guidelines with effect from April 1,2000 in the Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan 
(KVS) led to a widespread dislocation of teachers across the country. Many of them 
were transferred thousands of kilometers away from their place of residence and 
families. Many couples were also separated across thousands of kilometers. This 
caused widespread misery in the entire system. Hundreds of teachers resigned from the 
service, some were dismissed for their inability to join in remote places. The measure not 
only affected families but also deprived KVS of experienced teachers. The recent transfer 
guidelines of 7th July, 2004 have tried to address this problem and is helping people to 
come closer 
138 

[6 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
to their places of residence. The salient features of modified transfer guidelines are 
as under:— 
(i)   The concept of "displacement transfers" has been done away with. 
(ii)   The transfers should mostly be done only against vacancies on the basis of 
requests received for the same. 
(iii)  In general, teachers/staff members will not be transferred except on 
administrative grounds. 
(iv)   The concept of surplus teachers has been changed from the existing criteria 
of declaring the teachers with longest stay as surplus to the teachers with 
least number of years served in a particular Vidyalaya. 
(v)   In order to ensure that there is minimum disruption of teachers from 
Kendriya Vidyalayas, it has been decided that even in case of promotion 
of teachers, the teachers can continue to work in the same Vidyalaya 
provided there is a vacancy. In case there is no vacancy he/she can exercise 
his request for the nearest available vacancies. 
(vi)   In order to provide relief to teachers who resigns from the service or were 
dismissed following their inability to join in places of posting as a result of 
transfer guidelines of the year 2000, a Committee has been constituted to 
consider the appeals of such teachers. They can appeal before this 
committee latest by 15th December, 2004 and this committee would take 
a decision within a month after that. This humane approach in the current 
transfer policy has been widely appreciated and it is hoped that within a 
year or two the KVS will be able to redress the grievances, of all the 
affected teachers to a substantial extent.

Vulgarity on Cable TV and print media 
389. SHRIMATIPREMACARIAPPA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have devised any action plan or code of conduct for checking 
vulgarity on cable TV network and print media; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) and (b) The Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 prescribe that 
no programme shall be carried through Cable TV Network, provided it conforms to the 
Programme and Advertisement Codes as defined in the Cable Television Networks Rules, 
1994. The Programme and Advertisement Codes cited, inter alia, prohibit vulgarity through 
cable T.V. network. The Central Government has constituted an Inter-Ministerial 
Committee under Section 20 of the said Act to look into the violations of the Codes. 
Cognizance of any violations of the Codes is taken either suo-moto or on receipt of specific 
complaints by the Committee. Besides, any authorized officer under the aforesaid Act is 
empowered to prohibit any cable operator from transmitting or re-transmitting any 
programme or channel if it is not in conformity with the prescribed codes. A meeting is 
also proposed to be held shortly with stakeholders including women organizations, 
educations, consumer organisation with broadcasters, cable operators organisation etc., so that 
the matter can be sensitized on these issues. 
As regards print media, the Press in India is free from Government control. In 
pursuance of its policy to uphold the freedom of the Press, the Government does not 
interfere with its functioning. However, the Press Council of India is a statutory 
autonomous body set up under the Press Council Act, 1978 with the twin object of 
preserving the freedom of the Press and of maintaining and improving the standards of 
newspapers and 
148 

[6 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
news agencies in India. The Council has built "Norms of Journalistic 
Conduct", which, inter-alia, provide for obsenity and vulgarity to be 
eschewed and cover principles and ethics with regard to journalism.

Appraisal of Tenth Plan Report, Draft Chapter VIII). This is likely to increase to 50% or 
more in the forthcoming three years.

infrastructure in small and medium towns so as to arrest migration from these to large urban 
centres, while the Mega City Scheme seeks to augment/strengthen infrastructure in 
Mega Cities to cater to increase in population. 
(e) Providing housing, water, health, sanitation and other necessities is the primary 
responsibility of the State Governments/Union Territories. However, this Ministry has been

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION OF CHAIR 
Re: Non-payment Of Access Deficit Charges (ADC) By Private Telecom 
Operators 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, with a very heavy 
heart, I rise today to bring to the notice of the House and also the Government 
regarding the huge scam in the telecom sector that has been taking place for the 
last one year, or, maybe, even more. But, Sir, as somebody who has been 
associated with this House for creating a situation whereby universal telecom 
connectivity can be provided to the people of this country, I Find instances where 
institutions, which have been created through enactments by this august House, 
have criminally neglected their responsibility, in enforcing regulation and in due 
discharge of the legal powers that were provided to them. The result today, Sir, is 
that an amount of more than Rs. 2000 crores which was to be paid by certain 
private telecom operators to the Government and, through the Government, to the 
Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited, to provide telecom connectivity to backward rural 
areas, far-flung areas has not been paid. Sir, now it is common knowledge 
and it is part of the public domain that a prima facie case has been established in 
regard to non-payment of ADCs at the prescribed rates which were stipulated 
by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, and also through the order of the 
Government of India. Sir, the sordid story begins with having a telecom regulator 
that was pliant, that was close to the Government. I recall the proceedings of this 
House when initially we had created the TRAI; and many of the Members in the 
Government today were part of the process. 
Sir, in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of that Act, what we had 
provided for was that "TRAI will be set up for protection and promotion of 
consumer interest, and ensuring fair competition. There is a felt need to separate 
regulatory functions from service-providing functions, which will be in keeping with 
the general trend in the world." It further said, "in which the private operator will be 
competing with Government operators, there is a pressing need for an independent 
telecom regulatory body for regulation 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
of telecom services for orderly and healthy growth of telecommunication 
infrastructure, apart from protection of consumer interest." 
Now, Sir, I refer to the order of the Telecom Regulatory Authority that for every 
international call, the operators that were bringing in the international calls were 
supposed to pay Rs. 4.25 to the Government, which goes to the BSNL for 
providing telecom connectivity. Sir, the two consultation papers of the Telecom 
Regulatory Authority show — I do not, for the paucity of time, go into the specific 
orders; I have them with me — that this differential between access deficit charge, 
which was to be paid for national long distance calls and international long 
distance calls, created a situation whereby grey.market could emerge. The 
TRAI also, in the report of the Sub-Committee that it created, where it included 
representatives of the Government, of the public sector telecom operator as well as 
private sector companies, says that this a very serious situation and grey market 
has, indeed, emerged. 
Sir, the issue is not only non-payment of money; there is an element of national 
security also. This should be also taken note of by the hon. Finance Minister. Telecom 
today has security implications, and this has been noted by the Government of India 
in its order, which states that when the party is calling from a foreign land to our 
telephones, normally we should have the caller line identification appearing on our 
handsets. But they were tempered with by the private players to avoid paying the 
legitimate access deficit charges. Sir, I tested myself day before yesterday 
when I called some friend in England and I asked him to call back. I saw that 
there was no caller line identification still available on my handset. This is 15 days 
after the DoT has come out with a public advertisement in all Indian newspapers that 
when you see that there is no caller line identification appearing on your 
handsets, you shall understand that this is part of the whole imbroglio which leads to 
grey market and which leads to fleecing of public money. 
Now, I may say, Sir, that the appointment of the present regulator, present 
Chairman of the TRAI, has led to a decline in rural connectivity in terms of 
telecommunication in our country. I have the facts and figures with me. 
Actually, the telecom growth has led to tremendous inequities between the 
urban sector and the rural sector. Today, for every 1.6 telephones in the rural 
areas, there are 20 telephones in the urban areas, and the gap is widening; Sir, it is 
a shame that this is despite knowing that grey market will emerge. This is 
documented, in all these documents of TRAI consultation papers, as well as the 
Sub-Committee notes, and they

[6 Decern ber, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
say that they pose a very grave threat, and recommend the stringent of 
punishments like cancellation of ILD licence, and proceeding against them in 
accordance with national security laws. 
Sir, we are the only Parliament which was attacked by the terrorists, and 
whatever we could do in terms of investigation was on the basis of the CLI which 
was available from the telephones of the extremist elements and the terrorist 
elements who attacked the Parliament. Now, there is a very serious 
security breach. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That is enough. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, the Government of India, which had this 
responsibility, and which was in full knowledge of what was happening, should 
have, in public interest, directed the TRAI, as they are empowered under the TRAI 
Act, to undertake an investigation on the extent of scam; how much money has 
been fleeced; how much manipulation has taken place; and, who are 
responsible. Sir, as late as the 1st of December, the whole nation knew, through 
the Government's reply in the Lok Sabha, that the breach was only to the tune of 
Rs. 300 crores, whereas BSNL and MTNL, the two public sector telecom 
companies, have filed claims for about Rs. 600 crores. The Government is 
saying, "Only Rs. 300 crores", and this is a very serious issue. We are told; 
press reports are coming that the Ministry says that if they cancel the licence 
of all those private operators, the consumers will be affected which is a total 
untruth because in terms of inter national long distance operator licence 
cancellation, there is no effect on the subscribers because they are not access 
providers. Therefore, Sir, on the basis of the facts and documentary evidence 
available with me, I demand that the TRAI Chairman should immediately be sacked 
by the Government in public interest. This is a very serious issue. Secondly, 
the Government should institute a full-fledged inquiry into the whole scam which 
has led to fleecing money to the tune of more than Rs. 2000 crores which 
should have provided telephone coverage for the rural areas and far-flung areas 
which is the core commitment of the Common Minimum Programme. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Basu, that is enough. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, as a result of this, we want the most stringent 
punishment against all those private operators — I would not name any Single 
company because I am not against any single company— Who are involved in this 
and acted in criminal complicity.

distinct improvement. Despite the existing law that prohibited employment of 
scavengers, many States are yet to enforce it in true letter and spirit.

Demand for inquiry into Kanpur Airport incident in Kerala 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Sir, on 1st November, 2004, the 
supporters of a political party came as a procession to Karipur Airport to welcome 
a Minister of Kerala on his  arrival from abroad. These supporters unleashed attack on 
Media person who came to cover the arrival of Minister, without provocation. The 
crowd blocked all the entries to the airport causing a lot of inconvenience to the 
passengers. They also constructed a stage in the middle of the road leading to 
the airport premises and blocked the way. Due to these activities, so many 
passengers missed the flight to various destinations. 
These workers went to the extent of climbing on top of the airport terminal building 
and hoisted their flag on the top of it. This also points out to the fact that even 
the security of the airport was at stake. 
The Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Civil Aviation Act, 
1982, in Chapter II, Offences, clearly mentions regarding offence at Airport, that 
whoever commits and act of violence which is likely to cause grievous hurt or 
death of any person or endangering or threatening the safety of airport shall be 
punished with Imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine. 
As per the said Act, the Government have the power to authorise an officer 
to conduct investigation with powers of arrest and prosecution. 
Therefore, it is urged that an urgent inquiry as per the aforesaid Act be 
ordered. 
Sir, I would like to seek the response of the Government in this matter 
because I have ...(Interruptions).

problem ...(Interruptions). 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: No. I am seeking an inquiry under the Civil

Need for providing tetter equipment and Clothing, to Soldiers 
posted at Siachen and Kargil frontiers 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA(Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, 
we all acclaim the sacrifices made by our courageous soldiers at Saltoro 
Ridge overlooking Siachen, Hanif, Yaldor Sectors in Kargil and other frontiers 
of India where temperature goes down to -40 to -50 degrees. At the same 
time we are equally responsible for the pathetic conditions in which they 
have to guard our borders. They are performing their duty with old, torn, 
obsolete clothing in chilly 16,000 feet height Indian border. A proposal has 
been submitted for three sets of specialised clothing — one for troops 
posted there, one for soldiers to get acclimatize and the other for outfit 
soldiers who may have to rush in case of emergency — but the proposal 
is hanging fire. The problem is, so cruel are the conditions that barely 15% 
of the clothing and snow-boots can be reused. Then, many of these clothing 
such as Pitons, Carabineers, Down Jackets, Multi-tiered Insulating Gloves, 
Special Trousers, Woolen Socks, Goggles, Gore-Tex suit come from 
Switzerland, Boot Crampons, Rucks acks, Special Boots from Central 
Europe and Sleeping Bags from Belgium. If the Government shows any 
lethargy, things will go from bad to worse. Even the Subramanyaswami 
Committee recommended that priority should be given to equipping infantry 
men with superior equipment and clothing. Recently, i had personally seen 
the pathetic conditions under which our soldiers have to work at Siachen 
and Kargil. Hence, I demand that immediate steps should be taken and 
the equipments that I mentioned should be procured within no time and be 
supplied to the Army immediately. Thank you.

Sir, this is a non-controversial Bill. As you know, Sir, the Supreme Court of 
India delivered a judgement in which the Supreme Court held that a State 
Government did not have the power to notify an apex bank as a cooperative 
society, and, therefore, the Reserve Bank of India did not have the authority to 
license such an apex bank. We are trying to get over that lacuna. There are 34 
such multi-State cooperative societies which have been licensed by the RBI. We 
could not have left a vacuum. This judgement came in last year, in October, 2003. The 
then Government was considering amendments, but before the amendments 
could be moved, Parliament was dissolved, and there has been a change. So, 
we are introducing the Bill to fill that gap. Now, the Reserve Bank of India will have 
the authority to license multi-State cooperative societies. You will find in Section 
2(I)(A) of the Bill that all licences granted so far shall be deemed to have 
been validly granted. Secondly, we want the deposits of all these multi-State 
cooperative societies also to be eligible to be insured by the Deposit 
Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation. So, the Section is being 
amended to clarity that the deposits of these multi-State cooperative societies 
will also get the benefit of the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee 
Corporation Act. In order to effect these two changes, I am moving these 
amendments. This Bill was passed unanimously by all sections of the House 
in the Lok Sabha. I am sure, I will get unanimous support from all sections of 
the House.

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, regarding new section 36AAA in clause 2 of

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, there are two ways to look at it. If you make 
such very definite grounds, the Reserve Banks' powers get limited to the grounds 
which are mentioned with such specificity. I think, the safer approach is to have 
broad heads, but ensure that, within the Reserve Bank, there is a system 
which alerts the Reserve Bank to take action at an early stage. I think, the heads 
are very broad. The first head is public interest, the second head is preventing 
the affairs of a banks from being conducted in a manner detrimental to the 
interest of depositors, and the third head is proper management of the bank. 
These are broad heads. I think, this gives a much greater degree of latitude to 
the RBI, and any order passed by the RBI, cannot easily be challenged if the 
heads are broad. If the heads are limited, then one will be left with the situation 
where you cannot take action, except on that very specific head. I think, the 
point as well taken. Given this broad power, we must have a system within the RBI 
which acts early, rather than late, which strikes it incipient delinquency rather 
than terminal illness. But I will ensure that the RBI is apprised of this fact, and the
